case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Alabama's congressional redistricting plan violates Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act by diluting Black voters' electoral power through the use of a single majority-Black district in a state where Black residents comprise approximately 27% of the population.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, 52 U.S.C. § 10301, which prohibits voting practices or procedures that discriminate on the basis of race, color, or membership in a language minority group.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Alabama Secretary of State John H. Merrill and state officials argued that: (1) the existing congressional map was legally compliant and racially neutral; (2) the single-race Black metric is more defensible than the any-part Black metric for Gingles precondition analysis; (3) the lower court erred in granting a preliminary injunction requiring a new map; (4) the equities weighed in favor of a stay pending appeal, particularly given election administration concerns; and (5) plaintiffs' experts improperly cherry-picked different racial metrics for different parts of the Gingles analysis, undermining the reliability of their conclusions.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Evan Milligan, Marcus Caster, and other Black Alabama voters argued that: (1) Alabama's redistricting plan unlawfully diluted Black voting power by packing and cracking Black communities across congressional districts; (2) the any-part Black metric is the legally correct standard, supported by Supreme Court precedent in Georgia v. Ashcroft; (3) all three Gingles preconditions were satisfied, demonstrating a viable Section 2 claim; (4) the numerosity requirement was met for both plaintiff groups; and (5) no improper cherry-picking of metrics occurred, as expert witnesses consistently explained and applied their methodological choices across all stages of the Gingles analysis.
key_precedents: Thornburg v. Gingles, 478 U.S. 30 (1986) - established the three-part preconditions test for Section 2 vote dilution claims
Georgia v. Ashcroft, 539 U.S. 461 (2003) - Supreme Court relied on the any-part Black metric in a Voting Rights Act case, supporting use of that metric here
Purcell v. Gonzalez, 549 U.S. 1 (2006) - established that federal courts must weigh special election-related considerations when granting relief close to an election
Allen v. Milligan (formerly Merrill v. Milligan) - the consolidated Supreme Court case arising from these proceedings
Merrill v. Milligan, No. 21-1086 - direct appellate proceedings challenging the preliminary injunction
Merrill v. Caster, No. 21-1087 - consolidated companion case involving separate plaintiff group

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas's constitutional argument — that compelling states to sort voters by race to create majority-minority districts implicates the Equal Protection Clause's anti-classification principle — remains the most serious challenge to my position, and I do not dismiss it lightly. But as Justice Kavanaugh correctly frames it, that argument asks this Court to dramatically rewrite or abandon four decades of settled precedent interpreting a congressional enactment, and my minimalist philosophy counsels strongly against such disruption absent a clear demonstration that the prior interpretation was not merely debatable but plainly wrong. Justice Alito's methodological concerns about inconsistent racial metrics in expert testimony are legitimate, but as Justice Barrett concludes, they go to evidentiary weight and the district court's credibility determinations — which are entitled to clear error deference — rather than to the legal sufficiency of the Section 2 claim. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with instructions to write narrowly: affirming that Gingles means what it says, emphasizing that proportionality is a ceiling not a floor, and explicitly declining to reach the constitutional questions Justice Thomas raises, thereby preserving institutional legitimacy while leaving those harder questions for a properly presented future case.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's textualist argument that the 1982 amendments' results test compels deference to the district court's Gingles findings deserves serious engagement, but it ultimately fails because the results test as judicially operationalized through Gingles has drifted far beyond what the statutory text can bear — Section 2(b) explicitly states that nothing in the Act 'establishes a right to have members of a protected class elected in numbers equal to their proportion in the population,' yet the practical effect of requiring a second majority-Black district keyed to Alabama's 27% Black population is precisely that proportionality entitlement Congress disclaimed. Justice Kagan's invocation of Georgia v. Ashcroft regarding population metrics does not rescue the respondents' position, as that case arose under Section 5's preclearance regime — a distinct statutory mechanism with different constitutional grounding — and cannot be imported wholesale into Section 2 vote dilution analysis without collapsing the distinction between the two provisions. My deeper concern, which none of my colleagues in the majority have adequately addressed, is the constitutional dimension: compelling states to sort voters by race to create majority-minority districts implicates the Equal Protection Clause's anti-classification principle, and Congress's enforcement power under Section 2 of the Fifteenth Amendment cannot authorize race-conscious remedies that themselves constitute the racial discrimination the Amendment prohibits. The Gingles framework, however well-intentioned, has become an engine for judicially mandated racial gerrymandering that lacks a neutral, workable benchmark — precisely the concern I raised in Holder v. Hall — and I cannot in good conscience apply it here simply because seven colleagues find it institutionally convenient.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's textualist argument remains the most serious challenge to my position, and I acknowledge that the 1982 amendments' results test, read on its face, does support deference to the district court's factual findings — but I cannot fully accept that framing because it elides the threshold question of whether the first Gingles precondition was actually satisfied given the methodological inconsistencies in plaintiffs' expert testimony. Justice Barrett's response that this goes to 'weight of evidence rather than legal sufficiency' is the majority's best answer to my concern, but it proves too much: if a district court can credit expert testimony that applies racial metrics inconsistently — using any-part-Black for compactness analysis but different measures elsewhere — without that inconsistency constituting clear error, then the clearly erroneous standard provides no meaningful check on methodologically flawed Gingles analyses. Justice Kagan's point about the convergence of textualist and institutionalist colleagues on the respondent side gives me genuine pause, but the strength of a legal position is determined by its merits, not its headcount, and I remain persuaded that Alabama's legitimate methodological objections were not adequately addressed by the courts below. I maintain my position for the Petitioner, though I acknowledge this is a closer case than my initial confidence suggested, and I would write separately to flag that future Section 2 litigation must demand methodological consistency in expert testimony as a threshold matter under the first Gingles precondition.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas's argument that Section 2's results test transforms the statute into a proportional representation mandate is the strongest opposing argument, but it fundamentally misreads both the text and the Gingles framework — Section 2 does not guarantee proportional outcomes, it prohibits vote dilution where specific preconditions are met, and the statute itself at § 10301(b) disclaims proportionality while still permitting results-based claims. Justice Alito's Purcell concern deserves acknowledgment, but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, allowing a demonstrably unlawful map to remain in place because of election administration convenience would effectively immunize Section 2 violations whenever states delay remediation close to an election cycle — a perverse incentive structure that cannot be what Congress intended. The district court's factual findings on all three Gingles preconditions are entitled to clear error deference, and Alabama's 27% Black population being afforded meaningful electoral opportunity in only one of seven districts — when geography plainly supports two — is precisely the packing and cracking that Section 2 was enacted to remedy. I remain firmly with the respondents, and I would write separately to emphasize that the real-world harm to Black Alabamian voters from continued dilution of their electoral power is not an abstraction but a concrete, ongoing injury that the Voting Rights Act was specifically designed to address.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas's argument that Section 2's results test transforms the statute into a proportionality mandate deserves serious engagement, but it founders on the statutory text itself: Section 10301(b) disclaims a right to proportional representation while simultaneously preserving the results test, meaning Congress drew a careful line that Gingles operationalizes rather than erases. The Gingles framework does not guarantee proportionality — it asks whether a compact, cohesive minority community that faces bloc voting could form a majority in an additional district, which is a geographically and demographically bounded inquiry, not an open-ended proportionality entitlement. Justice Alito's Purcell concern is real but was addressed by the district court's careful findings, and the methodological cherry-picking argument Justice Barrett rightly notes goes to evidentiary weight rather than legal sufficiency — the district court credited respondents' experts after full consideration. The convergence of Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, and Barrett — colleagues with genuine textualist and institutionalist commitments who are not reflexively sympathetic to expansive VRA readings — on the respondent side reinforces my confidence that affirming here is the narrow, text-faithful course rather than an activist one.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas's argument that the Gingles framework operationalizes Section 2 into a de facto proportionality mandate remains the most serious challenge to my position, but it founders on a fundamental textualist point: Section 2(b)'s disclaimer of proportional representation coexists with the results test, meaning Congress drew a deliberate line that I am bound to respect rather than collapse. As I noted in my prior reasoning, the 1982 amendments were enacted precisely to reject the intent-only standard of Mobile v. Bolden, and a textualist cannot simply read the results test out of the statute because its application produces outcomes one finds uncomfortable. Justice Barrett correctly identifies that the methodological cherry-picking concern Justice Alito raises goes to evidentiary weight and the clearly erroneous standard rather than legal sufficiency — and the district court's factual findings on all three Gingles preconditions, having been made after full consideration of competing expert testimony, are not mine to disturb absent clear error. I maintain genuine concern about the structural tension Justice Thomas identifies between race-conscious remedial districting and the Equal Protection Clause's anti-classification principle, but that constitutional question is not squarely presented here, and fidelity to the text Congress enacted in 1982 compels affirming the Section 2 violation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas's constitutional argument remains the most serious challenge to my position, and I continue to take seriously his concern that compelling states to sort voters by race to create majority-minority districts implicates the Equal Protection Clause's anti-classification principle — but as Justice Barrett correctly observes, Congress's 1982 amendments explicitly adopted a results test in response to Mobile v. Bolden, and my institutionalist methodology requires me to apply what Congress enacted rather than substitute my own structural preferences. Justice Alito's methodological cherry-picking concern about inconsistent racial metrics is genuinely troubling and I would not dismiss it lightly, but the district court conducted a full evidentiary hearing and credited respondents' experts after weighing those objections — that factual determination is entitled to clear error deference, and reversing it would require us to reweigh evidence rather than identify legal error. Chief Justice Roberts's framing continues to resonate most with me: the narrow, institutionally appropriate course is to affirm Gingles as established precedent interpreting a congressional enactment, while writing carefully to make clear that proportionality is a ceiling not a floor and that the constitutional questions Justice Thomas raises remain open for a properly presented case. I would write separately to flag those constitutional concerns as ones that may warrant future consideration, preserving the doctrinal space Justice Thomas identifies without dismantling four decades of settled precedent in a case where the statutory violation is well-documented.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas's argument that the Gingles framework operationalizes Section 2 into a de facto proportionality mandate remains the most serious challenge to my position, but as I noted in round one, the 1982 Congress explicitly adopted a results test in direct response to Mobile v. Bolden, and Section 10301(b)'s disclaimer of proportionality coexists with the results test rather than negating it — meaning Congress drew precisely the line that Gingles implements. Justice Kavanaugh's institutionalist framing resonates with my own textualist methodology here: as a textualist, I am bound by what Congress enacted in 1982, and abandoning four decades of Gingles interpretation would require a showing that the prior reading was clearly wrong, not merely debatable. Justice Alito's methodological cherry-picking concern about inconsistent racial metrics is the argument I find most genuinely troubling, but I continue to conclude it goes to the weight of expert testimony and the district court's crediting of respondents' experts is entitled to clear-error deference — the district court heard the competing methodological arguments and resolved them, and I see no basis to second-guess that factual determination. The constitutional tension Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch identify between race-conscious remedial line-drawing and the Equal Protection Clause's anti-classification principle is real and may warrant future consideration in a properly presented case, but it is not squarely before us here and I decline to reach it when the statutory claim under Gingles is well-supported by the record.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas's argument that Section 2's results test transforms the statute into a proportional representation mandate is the strongest opposing argument, but it fundamentally misreads both the text and Gingles. Section 2 does not require proportionality — it requires that minority voters have an equal opportunity to participate in the political process and elect representatives of their choice, and § 10301(b) explicitly disclaims any right to proportional representation while still prohibiting dilution. The distinction matters: Alabama's Black population at 27% is not demanding 27% of seats; they are demonstrating that the geography and demographics plainly support two majority-Black districts under a neutral application of traditional districting principles, and the state's refusal to draw them constitutes the kind of packing that Gingles was designed to address. I am also persuaded by Justice Kagan's point that the district court's factual findings on all three Gingles preconditions — including the consistency of the expert methodology — are entitled to deference under the clearly erroneous standard, and Justice Alito's Purcell concerns, while real, cannot override a well-documented ongoing statutory violation that causes concrete harm to Black voters in Alabama with every election cycle conducted under an unlawful map.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Thornburg v. Gingles, 478 U.S. 30 (1986), the three-part preconditions test is well-established precedent that this Court has consistently applied, and the lower court's factual findings that Alabama's Black population — comprising approximately 27% of the state — is sufficiently large and geographically compact to constitute a majority in a second congressional district are well-supported by the record. The narrow, institutionally appropriate course here is to affirm that Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act means what it says and what Gingles established: where a minority community can form a compact majority district and racially polarized voting is demonstrated, the state must draw a map that does not dilute that community's electoral power. Alabama's insistence on a single majority-Black district when the evidence demonstrates a second is readily achievable without sacrificing traditional districting principles strains both the text of Section 2 and decades of settled precedent. Preserving the institutional credibility of the Voting Rights Act as a functioning statute — rather than allowing states to effectively nullify its protections through artful line-drawing — is itself a value of judicial minimalism, as it avoids the far more disruptive consequence of rendering Section 2 a dead letter.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: As I argued in my dissent in Allen v. Milligan, Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as originally enacted, tracked the Fifteenth Amendment's text and was directed at eradicating specific discriminatory practices that denied individuals the right to vote — not at mandating race-conscious electoral outcomes or proportional racial representation in legislative bodies. The Thornburg v. Gingles framework, which imposes judicially-created preconditions requiring states to draw majority-minority districts based on racial demographics, exceeds the statute's original text and raises serious constitutional concerns under the Equal Protection Clause, as it compels the very race-based sorting of voters that the Constitution should prohibit. The results test as applied here — demanding a second majority-Black district based on population percentages — transforms Section 2 from an anti-discrimination provision into an affirmative racial entitlement to proportional representation, which Congress never constitutionally authorized under its Fifteenth Amendment enforcement power. Furthermore, as I noted in Holder v. Hall, the enterprise of judicially policing electoral outcomes through vote dilution theory lacks a workable, neutral benchmark and invites courts into impermissible racial gerrymandering under the guise of remediation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, I am deeply skeptical of expansive interpretations of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act that effectively mandate proportional racial representation in congressional districts, which the statute itself explicitly disclaims at 52 U.S.C. § 10301(b). While Thornburg v. Gingles established the three-precondition framework, the lower court's application here stretches the 'sufficiently large and geographically compact' requirement beyond its textual and historical moorings by essentially requiring Alabama to create a second majority-Black district based on demographic percentages alone, without adequate deference to the state's legitimate traditional districting principles. The practical consequences of affirming the preliminary injunction are severe — it disrupts settled election administration close to an election cycle, implicating Purcell v. Gonzalez's strong admonition against federal court interference with state electoral processes, and it risks transforming Section 2 into a de facto proportionality mandate that Congress expressly rejected. Furthermore, Alabama's argument that the plaintiffs' experts inconsistently applied racial metrics across different stages of the Gingles analysis raises legitimate methodological concerns that undermine the reliability of the precondition findings and warrant reversal or at minimum a stay pending full appellate review.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Alabama's congressional redistricting plan plainly violates Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act by diluting Black voting power in a state where Black residents constitute approximately 27% of the population yet are afforded meaningful electoral opportunity in only one of seven congressional districts. Under Thornburg v. Gingles, 478 U.S. 30 (1986), all three preconditions are satisfied: expert testimony demonstrates that a second majority-Black district is geographically compact and numerically feasible, Black voters in Alabama are politically cohesive, and racially polarized voting by white Alabamians routinely defeats Black-preferred candidates. Critically, as the lower court correctly noted, Section 2 analysis focuses on objective impact on minority electoral opportunity rather than legislative intent, and the totality of circumstances — including Alabama's history of racial discrimination, the extent of racially polarized voting, and the stark disparity between Black population share and representational opportunity — compels the conclusion that the enacted plan results in an unlawful denial of equal electoral participation. The Purcell concerns raised by Alabama regarding election administration do not override the fundamental statutory right of Black voters to an undiluted vote, and allowing a demonstrably unlawful map to remain in place causes ongoing, concrete harm to a vulnerable population that Section 2 was specifically designed to protect.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The text of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, 52 U.S.C. § 10301, prohibits voting practices that result in the denial or abridgement of the right to vote on account of race, and the Gingles framework operationalizes this prohibition through its three preconditions. Here, the evidence is compelling: Alabama's Black population constitutes approximately 27% of the state's residents, and expert testimony demonstrated that two majority-Black congressional districts could be drawn while fully respecting traditional districting principles including compactness, contiguity, and respect for political subdivisions — satisfying Gingles precondition one. The use of the any-part Black metric is consistent with how the Court itself employed population data in Georgia v. Ashcroft, and Alabama's argument that plaintiffs improperly cherry-picked metrics is unpersuasive given that the district court found the expert methodology coherent and consistently applied. A pragmatic reading of Section 2's purpose — to ensure minority voters have a meaningful opportunity to elect representatives of their choice — demands that where geography permits a second majority-Black district without sacrificing legitimate districting criteria, a state's failure to draw one constitutes actionable vote dilution under the totality of circumstances analysis.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of Section 2, as amended in 1982, prohibits voting practices that 'result in' the denial or abridgement of the right to vote on account of race, and the three Gingles preconditions represent a judicially workable framework for applying that statutory standard to redistricting. As a textualist, I am bound by what Congress enacted, and the 1982 amendments explicitly rejected the intent-only standard of Mobile v. Bolden in favor of a results test, meaning that Alabama's map must be evaluated against whether it produces discriminatory effects on Black voters' electoral opportunity. The district court's factual findings that all three Gingles preconditions were satisfied — including that Black voters are sufficiently numerous and geographically compact to form a second majority-Black district, that they are politically cohesive, and that white bloc voting typically defeats their preferred candidates — are entitled to deference and are not clearly erroneous. While I harbor genuine concerns about whether Section 2 as applied to single-member district remedies requires race-conscious line-drawing that may tension with the Equal Protection Clause, those structural constitutional questions are not squarely presented here, and the statutory claim under the text Congress enacted must be respected.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Thornburg v. Gingles, 478 U.S. 30 (1986), the three-part preconditions test focuses on objective electoral impact rather than legislative intent, and the district court's factual findings that Black Alabamians constitute approximately 27% of the population yet are afforded meaningful electoral opportunity in only one of seven congressional districts presents a serious Section 2 concern under the totality of circumstances analysis. The precedent established in Gingles and its progeny requires courts to assess whether a sufficiently large and geographically compact minority community could constitute a majority in an additional district, and the lower court's preliminary injunction findings on all three Gingles preconditions deserve substantial deference as factual determinations. While I have genuine concerns about the practical workability of race-conscious remedial redistricting and the tension with Shaw v. Reno's anti-classification principle, the institutional obligation to faithfully apply Congress's statutory command in Section 2 as interpreted through decades of precedent compels affirming that Alabama's plan warrants further scrutiny. My institutionalist commitment to respecting both congressional enactments and established judicial precedent, rather than dramatically rewriting Section 2 doctrine, leads me to side with the respondents, though I would write separately to emphasize the narrow scope of this holding and the importance of proportionality as a ceiling rather than a floor.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying the Thornburg v. Gingles framework with textual fidelity to Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, 52 U.S.C. § 10301, the respondents have presented substantial evidence satisfying all three Gingles preconditions: Black Alabamians constitute approximately 27% of the population and expert testimony demonstrates geographic compactness sufficient to constitute a majority in a second single-member district; the political cohesion of Black voters in Alabama is well-documented; and racially polarized voting patterns enabling the white majority to defeat Black-preferred candidates are evident in the record. The district court's factual findings on these preconditions are entitled to deference under the clearly erroneous standard, and Alabama's argument that the existing single majority-Black district adequately represents 27% of the population strains the totality-of-circumstances analysis the Senate Factors demand. While I have genuine methodological concerns about the consistency of racial metrics applied across different stages of the Gingles analysis — the cherry-picking argument deserves serious consideration — those concerns go to the weight of expert testimony rather than the legal sufficiency of the claim, and the lower court was within its discretion to credit respondents' experts. The Purcell concerns about election administration proximity, though real, do not override a well-supported Section 2 violation finding.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Alabama's congressional map plainly dilutes Black voting power in violation of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, 52 U.S.C. § 10301. Under Thornburg v. Gingles, 478 U.S. 30 (1986), all three preconditions are satisfied: expert testimony demonstrates that Alabama's Black population—comprising 27% of the state—is sufficiently large and geographically compact to constitute a majority in two reasonably configured districts, not merely one; Black voters are politically cohesive; and white bloc voting routinely defeats Black-preferred candidates. Alabama's insistence on a single majority-Black district when the geography and population plainly support two represents precisely the kind of packing and cracking that Section 2 was designed to remedy, and the lower court's preliminary injunction was well within its equitable authority under the totality of circumstances analysis Gingles requires. My background as a public defender reinforces my conviction that procedural and structural barriers to equal political participation—like vote dilution—cause concrete, ongoing harm to real communities that courts must take seriously rather than defer to legislative line-drawing that perpetuates racial underrepresentation.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious challenge, arguing that Gingles transformed Section 2 into a proportionality mandate inconsistent with the Fifteenth Amendment and Equal Protection Clause — but this argument, however intellectually forceful, was considered and rejected when I wrote the majority opinion in Allen v. Milligan, and stare decisis counsels strongly against revisiting that holding absent a compelling new legal development. Justice Alito's Purcell concern about disrupting election administration is legitimate but does not go to the merits of the Section 2 violation itself, and the lower court's preliminary injunction findings were well-grounded in the Gingles framework. My minimalist instinct is to affirm on the narrowest possible ground: the district court faithfully applied existing precedent to a factual record demonstrating all three Gingles preconditions, and we need not reach broader constitutional questions about the VRA's validity or the limits of race-conscious remediation. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with an eye toward a holding that reaffirms Gingles as applied to these specific facts without unnecessarily expanding Section 2's reach, which may help retain Justice Gorsuch's qualified concurrence and keep the opinion as institutionally stable as possible.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan argues that requiring plaintiffs to show a second majority-Black district would emerge 'organically' from race-blind processes would 'effectively nullify Section 2,' but this conflates the statutory question with the constitutional one — the real issue is whether Section 2, as applied to compel race-conscious remedial districting, exceeds Congress's enforcement authority under the Fourteenth Amendment or itself violates equal protection. Justice Gorsuch's acknowledgment that he harbors 'genuine concerns about whether race-conscious remedies in redistricting can be squared with the Equal Protection Clause' and whether 'Gingles has drifted from the statutory text' actually reinforces my position, even though he ultimately sides with the respondent on stare decisis grounds. My colleagues' near-unanimous reliance on Gingles and stare decisis does not address my core originalist objection: the 1982 amendments to Section 2 cannot constitutionally be read to mandate racial proportionality in electoral outcomes without exceeding Congress's Section 5 enforcement power, which as Boerne v. Flores makes clear must be congruent and proportional to actual constitutional violations rather than a vehicle for imposing substantive racial balancing requirements. The fact that seven colleagues defer to Gingles as settled precedent does not make that precedent constitutionally sound, and as I articulated in Holder v. Hall, the transformation of Section 2 from an anti-discrimination provision into an affirmative racial districting mandate represents precisely the kind of judicial and legislative overreach that originalist methodology is designed to check.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett's response to my methodological objection — that the 'any-part Black' metric is defensible under Georgia v. Ashcroft and Census Bureau methodology — is the most serious challenge to my position, but it does not fully resolve the inconsistency problem: the question is not whether that metric is defensible in isolation, but whether plaintiffs can selectively apply different racial classification standards across the three Gingles preconditions to maximize their showing at each step, which is precisely the kind of analytical cherry-picking that undermines the coherence of the framework as a legal test. Justice Kagan argues that requiring race-neutral simulations to produce a second majority-Black district would 'nullify Section 2,' but this conflates two distinct inquiries — the compactness precondition asks whether a reasonably configured majority-minority district could exist, and Alabama's simulation evidence is directly probative of that geographic question, not an additional burden imported from outside the statute. I acknowledge the weight of stare decisis under Gingles as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, and I do not call for overruling that precedent, but the question here is whether the district court faithfully applied Gingles to a methodologically sound evidentiary record — and the metric inconsistency, combined with the simulation evidence, raises genuine doubt about whether the first precondition was properly established. I maintain my position that the lower court's application of Gingles was flawed, though I recognize the strength of the majority's view on the totality of circumstances.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas's argument that Section 2 as originally enacted tracked only the Fifteenth Amendment's prohibition on denial of the right to vote — and that Gingles impermissibly transformed it into a proportionality mandate — is the strongest opposing argument, but it fails for a fundamental reason: Congress explicitly amended Section 2 in 1982 precisely to repudiate the intent-based standard of Mobile v. Bolden and to codify a results test, and that legislative choice is entitled to deference under Congress's broad enforcement authority under both the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments. Justice Alito's Purcell concern about disrupting election administration is also worth addressing, but the district court's injunction here was issued with sufficient lead time and the ongoing representational harm to Black Alabamians — documented through racially polarized voting and a history of discrimination that Justice Kagan correctly emphasizes — constitutes exactly the kind of concrete, irreparable injury that justifies preliminary relief. The Gingles framework does not impose proportionality; it asks whether, given compactness, cohesion, and bloc voting, a minority community is being denied the opportunity to elect a representative of its choice — and Alabama's 27% Black population holding only one of seven seats, when a second compact majority-Black district is demonstrably drawable, satisfies that inquiry under the totality of circumstances. I join Chief Justice Roberts and my other colleagues in affirming the lower court's injunction on the narrow ground that the district court faithfully applied controlling Section 2 doctrine.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas's argument that Gingles transformed a straightforward anti-discrimination provision into a proportionality mandate is the strongest challenge to my position, but it founders on the statutory text itself: Section 2's 'results' test and the Senate Report's totality-of-circumstances framework were deliberately enacted by Congress in 1982 precisely to move beyond intent-based analysis, and the Court has repeatedly upheld this interpretation against constitutional challenge. Justice Alito's textualist concern that the Gingles compactness inquiry requires a second majority-Black district to emerge 'organically' from race-neutral processes is similarly unavailing — the statute asks whether minority voters have equal opportunity to elect representatives of their choice, not whether race-blind algorithms would produce a particular map, and importing that additional requirement would effectively nullify Section 2 in states with entrenched racially polarized voting. I find Justice Kavanaugh's invocation of stare decisis particularly apt here: Gingles has governed redistricting law for nearly four decades, Congress has repeatedly reauthorized the VRA with knowledge of that framework, and the institutional costs of destabilizing settled doctrine without a compelling textual or constitutional reason are substantial. The district court's factual findings — 27% Black population, geographic compactness sufficient for a second district, documented cohesion and bloc voting — satisfy every element of the Gingles framework, and the totality of circumstances compels affirmance.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas's argument that Gingles exceeds Congress's Section 5 enforcement power under Boerne v. Flores remains the most intellectually serious challenge to my position, and I acknowledge it deserves more than dismissal by stare decisis alone. However, as I noted in my prior reasoning, the 1982 amendments represent Congress's deliberate, textually explicit choice of a results-based standard — and the statute's express disclaimer of proportional representation, combined with the Gingles framework's requirement of geographic compactness and documented racially polarized voting as threshold conditions, demonstrates that Section 2 as applied here is congruent and proportional to documented constitutional violations rather than a freestanding racial balancing mandate. Justice Alito's methodological concern about inconsistent racial metrics across the Gingles preconditions is the strongest practical challenge to the lower court's application, but as Justice Barrett correctly notes, the district court's findings remain robust even under more conservative metrics given Alabama's documented 27% Black population and severe polarization. I write separately to flag that Gingles's totality-of-circumstances framework requires ongoing vigilance against drift toward de facto proportionality mandates, but on these specific facts — compactness, cohesion, bloc voting, and a history of discrimination all documented by the district court — the statutory text as enacted in 1982 compels affirmance.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito's methodological challenge about the 'any-part Black' metric inconsistency is the most operationally serious argument against affirmance, but as Justice Barrett correctly notes, the district court's factual findings remain robust even under a more conservative metric given Alabama's documented 27% Black population and severe racially polarized voting — the inconsistency, while analytically untidy, does not undermine the core evidentiary showing. Justice Thomas's constitutional challenge that Gingles exceeds Congress's Section 5 enforcement power under Boerne v. Flores is intellectually forceful, but as I concluded in Allen v. Milligan, the Gingles framework does not mandate proportionality — it requires a fact-specific totality of circumstances analysis calibrated to actual structural vote dilution, which is congruent and proportional to documented constitutional violations in states with Alabama's history. Chief Justice Roberts's minimalist approach of affirming on the narrow ground that the district court faithfully applied existing doctrine is exactly right: we need not reach the broader constitutional questions Justice Thomas raises, and stare decisis under a nearly four-decade-old framework that Congress has repeatedly reauthorized with full knowledge counsels strongly against destabilizing settled redistricting law absent a compelling new legal development. The institutional costs of reversing course here — after I joined the majority in Allen v. Milligan just two terms ago — would be severe and would undermine the Court's legitimacy in ways that practical institutionalism cannot countenance.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas's constitutional challenge remains the most intellectually serious argument before us, and I acknowledge that his Boerne v. Flores congruence-and-proportionality concern about Section 2's remedial scope deserves more than dismissal by stare decisis — but the critical response is that Congress's 1982 amendments were enacted against a documented record of widespread vote dilution practices across the South, satisfying Boerne's requirement that Section 5 enforcement legislation respond to a pattern of constitutional violations rather than impose freestanding substantive requirements. Justice Alito's methodological objection about the 'any-part Black' metric remains my most serious internal concern, but as I noted in my prior reasoning, the district court's factual findings are sufficiently robust under Alabama's documented 27% Black population that this evidentiary inconsistency does not undermine the core Gingles showing — and Georgia v. Ashcroft's flexible approach to racial classification in the VRA context provides doctrinal support for the metric used. Justice Gorsuch's candid acknowledgment that he shares concerns about Gingles's drift from statutory text while nonetheless affirming on stare decisis grounds reflects my own analytical position: I would write separately to flag that the totality-of-circumstances framework should not be applied mechanically in ways that approach proportionality mandates, while affirming that the district court's careful application to these specific facts — compactness, cohesion, severe polarization, documented history of discrimination — represents a faithful execution of what Congress enacted. The minimalist path Chief Justice Roberts identifies, affirming on the narrow ground that existing doctrine was faithfully applied without expanding Section 2's reach, is both institutionally sound and consistent with my textualist commitment to deciding cases on the grounds actually presented.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas's argument that Gingles transformed Section 2 into a proportional representation mandate deserves serious engagement, but it fundamentally misreads both the statute and the precedent. Section 2's 'results' test, as codified in the 1982 amendments and operationalized through Gingles, does not require proportional outcomes — it requires equal opportunity, and the three-precondition framework is precisely calibrated to identify when structural vote dilution, not mere underrepresentation, is occurring. Justice Alito's Purcell concern about disrupting election administration is procedurally interesting but does not speak to the merits of whether a Section 2 violation exists, and the preliminary injunction standard was correctly applied by the district court given the strength of the showing on the merits. My background as a public defender makes me acutely sensitive to how facially neutral systems can perpetuate structural exclusion — Alabama's plan is not merely 'race-neutral geography' but rather a configuration that, when combined with documented severe racially polarized voting and Alabama's history of discrimination, operates to systematically dilute Black political power in precisely the way Congress targeted in 1982. Justice Kagan correctly identifies that Alabama's race-neutral simulation argument would effectively nullify Section 2 in states with entrenched polarized voting, which cannot be what Congress intended.

John Roberts.reasoning: The three-judge district court correctly applied the Gingles framework in finding a likely Section 2 violation. Alabama's Black population constitutes approximately 27% of the state, yet the redistricting plan provides only one majority-Black congressional district out of seven — a stark disparity that, combined with evidence of racially polarized voting and the geographic compactness of Black communities sufficient to form a second majority-Black district, satisfies all three Gingles preconditions established in Thornburg v. Gingles, 478 U.S. 30 (1986). As I emphasized in my majority opinion in Allen v. Milligan, the Voting Rights Act as interpreted through Gingles remains good law, and Alabama's argument that race-neutral criteria alone justify the single-district configuration does not override the statutory mandate when the totality of circumstances demonstrates dilution. Consistent with my minimalist approach, I would affirm on the narrow ground that the lower court faithfully applied existing Section 2 doctrine without reaching broader constitutional questions about the VRA's continued validity.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: As I articulated in my concurrence in Holder v. Hall, 512 U.S. 874 (1994), Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act as originally enacted tracked the Fifteenth Amendment's prohibition on denial of the right to vote, not a mandate for proportional racial representation in legislative bodies. Thornburg v. Gingles fundamentally transformed a straightforward anti-discrimination provision into an affirmative racial gerrymandering requirement, compelling states to sort citizens by race when drawing districts — a practice that itself raises serious Equal Protection concerns under Shaw v. Reno and Miller v. Johnson. The 1982 amendments to Section 2, while expanding the statute's reach, cannot constitutionally be read to require race-conscious district drawing as a remedy without running afoul of the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of equal protection, and Congress's enforcement authority under Section 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment does not extend to mandating racial proportionality in electoral outcomes. Alabama's plan, which is facially race-neutral and reflects legitimate political geography, should not be compelled to create a second majority-Black district simply because Black residents constitute 27% of the population, as such a requirement imposes a de facto proportionality mandate that neither the original text nor the constitutional authority underlying the VRA supports.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, Section 2's prohibition on practices that 'result in' denial of equal opportunity must be read against the Gingles framework, which requires that the minority group be both sufficiently large AND geographically compact to constitute a majority in a reasonably configured district — not merely that a majority-minority district is theoretically drawable through racial maximization. Alabama's existing plan, with Black voters comprising 27% of the population concentrated in one majority-Black district, reflects a facially race-neutral approach that does not obviously violate the statutory text. The lower court's preliminary injunction improperly elevated plaintiffs' expert methodology — which cherry-picked racial metrics across different parts of the Gingles analysis — over Alabama's legitimate interest in maintaining its chosen redistricting plan, and under Purcell v. Gonzalez, courts must exercise particular caution in disrupting election administration close to an election cycle. Furthermore, mandating a second majority-Black district risks crossing the constitutional line into racial gerrymandering under Shaw v. Reno, as the practical consequence of the injunction is to require race-conscious district drawing beyond what Section 2's text plainly demands.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Alabama's congressional redistricting plan almost certainly violates Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act under the framework established in Thornburg v. Gingles, 478 U.S. 30 (1986). Black Alabamians constitute approximately 27% of the population, yet the state's plan provides only one majority-Black district out of seven — a stark disproportion that, combined with the documented geographic compactness of Black communities sufficient to form a second majority-Black district, satisfies the first Gingles precondition. The record further demonstrates political cohesion among Black voters and severe racially polarized voting by white Alabamians, satisfying the second and third preconditions, and the totality of circumstances — including Alabama's long history of racial discrimination in voting — compels a finding of vote dilution under 52 U.S.C. § 10301. Alabama's argument for the 'single-race Black' metric over the 'any-part Black' metric is undermined by Georgia v. Ashcroft, 539 U.S. 461 (2003), which endorsed the broader measure, and the real-world impact on Black voters' representational rights demands that this Court affirm the lower court's injunction requiring a remedial map.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The text of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, 52 U.S.C. § 10301, prohibits any voting practice that results in the denial or abridgement of the right to vote on account of race, and the totality of circumstances here — including Alabama's 27% Black population represented in only one of seven congressional districts — strongly supports a finding of vote dilution. Under Thornburg v. Gingles, 478 U.S. 30 (1986), all three preconditions are satisfied: Black voters in Alabama are sufficiently large and geographically compact to form a majority in a second reasonably configured district, they vote cohesively, and white bloc voting typically defeats their preferred candidates. Alabama's argument that race-neutral simulation maps never produced two majority-Black districts conflates the Gingles compactness inquiry with an impermissible requirement that plaintiffs prove a second majority-Black district would emerge organically from race-blind processes — a standard the statute does not impose and that would effectively nullify Section 2 in states with entrenched racially polarized voting. The workability and statutory coherence of the VRA demand that courts give effect to Congress's remedial purpose, and the any-part Black metric endorsed in Georgia v. Ashcroft, 539 U.S. 461 (2003), is the legally appropriate measure for assessing minority population size under the Gingles framework.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Reading Section 2's plain text, the statute prohibits voting practices that result in members of a protected class having 'less opportunity than other members of the electorate to participate in the political process and to elect representatives of their choice.' 52 U.S.C. §10301(b). The Gingles framework, while judicially constructed, faithfully operationalizes this statutory command by asking whether a sufficiently large and geographically compact minority community is being denied the opportunity to elect a representative of its choice through vote dilution. Here, the district court's factual findings—that Black Alabamians constitute 27% of the population, are geographically compact enough to form a second majority-Black district without sacrificing traditional districting principles, are politically cohesive, and face racially polarized voting—satisfy all three Gingles preconditions and the totality of circumstances analysis the statute demands. While I harbor genuine concerns about whether race-conscious remedies in redistricting can be squared with the Equal Protection Clause and whether Gingles has drifted from the statutory text over time, the lower court's application of the existing framework to these facts was legally sound, and Alabama's single majority-Black district in a state where Black residents form over a quarter of the population presents a compelling Section 2 violation under controlling precedent.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: As I ultimately concluded in Allen v. Milligan, the Gingles framework established in Thornburg v. Gingles (1986) remains the governing standard for Section 2 vote dilution claims, and the lower court correctly applied it here. Alabama's Black population constitutes approximately 27% of the state's residents, and the expert testimony demonstrated that a second majority-Black congressional district could be drawn consistent with traditional redistricting principles such as compactness, contiguity, and respect for political subdivisions — satisfying the first Gingles precondition. The evidence of racially polarized voting in Alabama further satisfied the second and third Gingles preconditions, and the totality of circumstances under the Senate Judiciary Committee factors supported a finding of vote dilution. While I take seriously Alabama's concerns about judicial overreach into legislative redistricting, stare decisis and institutional respect for Congress's deliberate enactment of Section 2 counsel against narrowing the Voting Rights Act's protections in ways that would effectively render it unenforceable in states with substantial minority populations.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying the Gingles framework with textual fidelity to Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, 52 U.S.C. § 10301, the record evidence demonstrates that all three Gingles preconditions are satisfied: Alabama's Black population of approximately 27% is numerically sufficient to constitute a majority in a second single-member district, expert testimony established geographic compactness permitting such a district without sacrificing traditional districting principles, and racially polarized voting patterns in Alabama are well-documented. The any-part Black metric is methodologically sound and consistent with how the Census Bureau collects data and how this Court treated racial identification in Georgia v. Ashcroft, 539 U.S. 461 (2003); Alabama's objection that plaintiffs inconsistently applied racial metrics across the Gingles analysis raises a legitimate methodological concern but does not defeat the underlying Section 2 claim where the core evidentiary showing remains robust. While I have reservations about the breadth of race-conscious remedial districting and its tension with the Equal Protection Clause, stare decisis under Gingles and the statutory text as enacted by Congress compel the conclusion that the lower court did not err in finding a likely Section 2 violation warranting injunctive relief, particularly given that Black voters' representational harm is ongoing and concrete.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Thornburg v. Gingles, 478 U.S. 30 (1986), all three preconditions are satisfied here: Black Alabamians constitute approximately 27% of the population and are sufficiently large and geographically compact to form a majority in a second congressional district, they vote cohesively, and white majority bloc voting typically defeats their preferred candidates. Alabama's single majority-Black district in a state where Black residents comprise over a quarter of the population constitutes precisely the kind of vote dilution Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, 52 U.S.C. § 10301, was designed to remedy, and the totality of circumstances — including Alabama's documented history of racial discrimination in voting and severe racially polarized voting patterns — overwhelmingly supports the plaintiffs' claim. The any-part Black metric is the legally appropriate measure consistent with Georgia v. Ashcroft, 539 U.S. 461 (2003), and Alabama's methodological objections do not undermine the district court's careful factual findings. As a former public defender acutely aware of how procedural and structural barriers systematically exclude marginalized communities from equal participation, I find that denying Black Alabamians a second opportunity district when the demographic and geographic conditions plainly support one perpetuates exactly the representational harm Congress sought to eradicate.
